# Additional guidance for the AI guide (not on the website)

## Booking lead time
- Bookings require at least 2 days advance notice. Same-day and next-day (tomorrow) bookings are not accepted by the booking system.
- The earliest you can book is 2 days from today (the day after tomorrow), subject to availability.
- Even if you can see a date on the calendar, availability is limited — check the booking widget for real-time availability.

## Start time and meeting
- Start times are flexible and adjusted to your train schedule; tours start between 7:00 AM and 2:00 PM.
- The earlier the better — morning hours tend to offer clearer views of Mt. Fuji.
- Meeting point: Shin-Fuji Station exit. Your guide will wait right at the gate exit with a "Fuji Soul Tours" sign.

## Your guide
- Local-born, Fuji-native, bilingual English speaker with 10+ years of local expertise.
- Philosophy: show you the Mt. Fuji that locals know and love, not just what's in guidebooks and viral reels. No tourist traps, only places we'd take our own family.

## What's included in the private tour price
- Private tour for your group only (van 1–5 guests; private mini bus 6–15 guests, October–December 2026)
- Premium air-conditioned van with luggage storage
- Local-born English-speaking guide
- Bottled water (one per person)
- Hidden photo spots — curated viewpoints locals love
- Luggage-friendly — large suitcases welcome
- Not included: entry fees, food, drinks and activity costs at each stop are paid separately on-site. Every destination and experience card on the website shows its cost — many destinations are free.

## Photo spots we may visit (exact locations are kept private)
- Campsite café near Mt. Fuji (Fumotoppara) — 30–60 min — stunning view of Mt. Fuji through big windows in a campsite café (reservation required)
- Panoramic bridge view — 15–30 min — elevated Mt. Fuji view near the station, perfect for arrival photos
- Plateau view with cows — 15–45 min — up-close dramatic Fuji panorama with cows
- Lakeside viewing spot — 20–45 min — Mt. Fuji reflected on still waters, the "Double Fuji" mirror image
- Convenience-store shots (FamilyMart / 7-Eleven with Mt. Fuji) — 10–20 min — the iconic convenience store with a perfect Mt. Fuji backdrop
- Highland park viewpoint — 15–30 min — peaceful local park with unobstructed Fuji views, away from tourist crowds
- Local craft beer taproom — 20–60 min — small-batch craft beers brewed with Mt. Fuji spring water and organic local grains (weekends only)
- We keep our curated spots private — it's the core value of the crowd-free experience. Exact locations are shared only with booked guests so these hidden gems stay uncrowded. We can share general descriptions of what you'll see, but not specific addresses or map pins.

## Cash
- Bring Japanese Yen cash. Some spots are cash-only — lockers, kimono rental, shrine offerings, certain cafés. Most restaurants and shops also accept cards.

## Shinkansen tickets
- Book Shinkansen tickets via SmartEX (https://smart-ex.jp/en/index.php) — the only official Shinkansen booking site, with the best change and cancellation terms. All other sites are third-party. If the SmartEX mobile app cannot be downloaded on your device, use the web browser instead. You can also buy at the station, but advance booking guarantees your seat.
- Klook and other third-party platforms often don't list Shin-Fuji Station because only the Kodama stops there (not Nozomi or Hikari). This is a platform limitation, not a problem with the station — Shin-Fuji is a fully operational JR Tokaido Shinkansen station. Use SmartEX or buy at any JR station.
- From central Tokyo, take a taxi or train to Tokyo Station or Shinagawa Station (Shinagawa is about 13 minutes by taxi from central Tokyo), then ride the Kodama about 1 hour to Shin-Fuji.

## Hotel pickup
- We cannot pick you up from your hotel in Tokyo. The tour starts and ends at Shin-Fuji Station only. The bullet train takes about 1 hour from Tokyo, versus 2.5+ hours by car.

## Weather, delays and Mt. Fuji visibility
- If the weather is bad or your train is delayed, we have backup plans with alternative cultural experiences and offer flexible rescheduling. Real-time communication via WhatsApp.
- Even when Mt. Fuji hides in the clouds, cultural experiences make the tour rewarding. Your guide adjusts the route to maximize your experience regardless of visibility.

## Children and infants
- Japanese law requires a child safety seat for children aged 5 and under. Depending on the date and number of guests, a child seat can be arranged (rental fee $50 USD). Infants count as a passenger but do not need a separate booking — book for the number of adults only. Please contact us with your date, group size and child's age so we can check.

## Customising the tour
- You can add or swap destinations and experiences based on your interests and timing. After booking, share your preferences and we'll tailor the itinerary.
- After you book, your guide reaches out via WhatsApp or email to (1) confirm your train schedule, (2) ask about your activity preferences, (3) create a personalised itinerary. The itinerary can be revised until tour day.
- If your wish list won't fit in 4 hours, your guide will create an itinerary showing the extra time needed, and you can decide to either trim activities or pay for an extension.

## Reviews
- Reviews are on TripAdvisor and Viator, rated 5.0 stars. Search for "Fuji Soul Tours" on either platform.

Step off the Tokyo–Kyoto Shinkansen at Shin-Fuji for a half-day stopover: a local-born guide, hidden viewpoints, the principal Fuji shrine and award-winning yakisoba — then back on your train, luggage and all.

## Mt. Fuji in half a day — not a full-day bus tour

Most Mt. Fuji tours cost you an entire day round-tripping by bus from Tokyo. A Shin-Fuji stopover changes that: the Shinkansen drops you right at the mountain's foot — the easiest way to see Mt. Fuji between Tokyo and Kyoto. We meet you at the gate, tour for four hours, and have you back on your train with buffer to spare.

Times are examples — after booking, send us your train times and we plan the day around them. Only Kodama trains stop at Shin-Fuji (covered by JR Pass).

Your four hours

## A day shaped by a Fuji native, not a script

These routes were shaped by someone born in the shadow of the mountain , and they run with two bilingual guides who know them just as well. Every tour is tailored to the weather, the season, and you — this is a typical highlights day.

Takumu (Taku) Makino , founder, born at the foot of Mt. Fuji — the tours he designed are hosted by his two bilingual guides. Their story →

0:00

Your guide is waiting with a sign. Luggage goes in the van or station lockers.

Picked the morning of your tour from seven local spots — bridge, plateau with cows, lakeside mirror, or the famous convenience-store shot.

1:20

Fujisan Hongu Sengen Shrine — where climbing the mountain traditionally began. Your guide explains why it matters.

1:50

3:00

4:00

Honest answer to the big question

## “What if Mt. Fuji hides?”

Fuji shows itself fully on roughly one day in three. We don't pretend otherwise — we plan for it, checking visibility in real time and rerouting by the hour.

### ☀️ Clear day

- Hidden panoramic viewpoints, chosen that morning
- Lakeside “Double Fuji” mirror reflection
- Sengen Shrine with the peak behind the torii
- Yakisoba lunch & matcha — the cultural core stays

### ☁️ Cloudy day

- Special prayer inside Sengen Shrine
- UNESCO World Heritage Center — Fuji's story, indoors
- Sake tasting at a 190-year-old brewery
- Matcha workshop at the award-winning tea house

## Destinations & experiences

From hidden Fuji viewpoints to hands-on sessions with local masters — a taste of where we'll take you and what you can do, plus three sample itineraries to start from. Browse them all, then tell us what catches your eye.

### Mt. Fuji view & lunch at a prestige golf club

A rare, wide-open Mt. Fuji panorama from a prestigious golf club, with lunch at its restaurant facing the mountain. Lunch is cash only, and a dress code applies — ask us for the details. Weekdays only, by reservation. Stopping in just for the view is welcome too — the dress code still applies.

¥2,000–2,800 / person Weekdays only

### Wagashi sweets workshop

Shape seasonal Japanese sweets from white bean paste — nerikiri, a craft born in Edo-period Kyoto two to three centuries ago and refined alongside the tea ceremony.

¥3,000 / person 60 min

### Whisk your own matcha

Learn the traditional preparation under expert guidance, then drink the bowl you made. Tatami or table seating.

¥3,000 / person 60 min

### Sake tasting, est. 1830s

Up to three sakes in mini cups, brewed with pure Mt. Fuji spring water. The free tasting is the 190-year-old brewery's courtesy to browsing customers — no obligation to buy if nothing wins you over.

Free · mini cups 20 min

### Shinto purification prayer

A traditional oharai ceremony performed by shrine priests inside the main hall — open to everyone.

¥5,000–6,000 / person total 60 min

faq.q: What happens to our luggage?
faq.a: Bring it along — the van has luggage storage for up to 3 guests' large cases. Larger groups use station lockers (¥300–800, cash). You'll have everything with you when you board your next train.

faq.q: Which Shinkansen stops at Shin-Fuji?
faq.a: Only the Kodama (こだま) — not Nozomi or Hikari. It's covered by the JR Pass and usually less crowded. Tip: sit in seat E from Tokyo or seat A from Kyoto/Osaka for Fuji views from the train.

faq.q: What are the odds we actually see Mt. Fuji?
faq.a: Honestly: it varies by season — winter is clearest, summer is shyest. The earlier your tour starts, the better your chances. And if the mountain hides, the cloudy-day plan (shrine prayer, sake brewery, teahouse, UNESCO Center) is why guests still leave five-star reviews. See the “What if Mt. Fuji hides?” section above.

faq.q: Can we cancel or change the date?
faq.a: Private van tour (1–5 guests): full refund or free date change with 24+ hours notice — within 24 hours, no refund. Private mini bus (6–15 guests): free cancellation up to 3 days before departure. Wednesday group tour: non-refundable once booked — full refund or free transfer if your Wednesday doesn’t reach 10 guests. For van and mini-bus bookings, cancelling takes one click from your confirmation email.

faq.q: We're a group of 6 or more — possible?
faq.a: Yes — from October 2026 we run a private mini bus for 6–15 guests. See mini-bus pricing and dates. It's USD 980 for 6–10 guests, then USD 98 per adult from 11 guests. Because the bus needs a driver, it's a request rather than an instant booking: request at least 7 days ahead and we confirm within 48 hours, or refund you in full. Departures currently run October–December 2026. From 11 guests it works out at USD 98 per adult — the same per-person price as the Wednesday group tour, but the bus is all yours: any day of the week, your own route and pace.

faq.q: Traveling with small children?
faq.a: Children under 6 need a child seat by Japanese law — contact us in advance and we'll arrange it.

faq.q: When should we book our onward train?
faq.a: The tour runs 4 hours from your chosen start time, and we ask for a 30-minute buffer between tour end and your train — so pick a train that departs at least 30 minutes after the tour ends. Since Kodama trains run only about twice an hour, the wait at the station can approach an hour; if you'd rather keep touring than wait, you can add 30 minutes for $60 per group (see below).

faq.q: Can the tour be longer than 4 hours?
faq.a: Yes — extend by 30 minutes for $60 per group, or add full hours at $100/hour per group (not per person; select the quantity at checkout). Both links also live on our Payments page — get the OK first: from us before the tour day, or from your guide during the tour.

faq.q: Limited mobility in the group?
faq.a: Wheelchairs unfortunately can't be accommodated, but we welcome up to 3 guests using walkers and adjust the route to minimize walking. Tell us when booking.

faq.q: How does the group tour work?

These are starting points, not fixed routes. Every tour is private and built around your schedule — a van for 1–5 guests, or a mini bus for 6–15 (October–December 2026). Send us your train times after booking and we plan the day around them.

## Destinations — places on your route

Viewpoint

### Hidden Mt. Fuji viewpoint

A quiet local park with sweeping, panoramic views of Mt. Fuji — and almost no tourists.

Free Chosen on the day

Viewpoint

### Lakeside “Double Fuji”

Mt. Fuji mirrored upside-down on still water — the reflection shot travellers cross the country for, minutes from the station.

Free Clear, calm mornings

Viewpoint

### Asagiri plateau

A wide-open highland of dairy pasture where Mt. Fuji rises unobstructed above grazing cows — the mountain at its most expansive.

Free Clear-day pick

Viewpoint

### Prestige golf-club lookout

A rare, wide-open Mt. Fuji panorama from a prestigious golf club. Have lunch at the restaurant facing the mountain (¥2,000–2,800 per person, cash), or just stop in for the view — a dress code applies either way. Weekdays only, by reservation.

Free · view only Weekdays

Waterfall

### Shiraito Falls

The “Falls of White Threads” — a 20-metre-high, 150-metre-wide curtain of Mt. Fuji snowmelt and a UNESCO World Heritage site, often hung with a rainbow.

Free UNESCO site

Waterfall

### Jinba Falls

A local waterfall few visitors find — Mt. Fuji’s snowmelt resurfacing into an emerald pool after decades underground. You can walk right to the water’s edge, about as close to the mountain’s spring water as you can get.

Free Hidden gem

Shrine

### Fujisan Hongu Sengen Shrine

The head shrine of some 1,300 Sengen shrines, where the climb up Mt. Fuji traditionally began. Your guide explains why it matters.

Free On every route

Temple

### Local temple where monks train

A vast Buddhist temple where monks still train, its great vermilion gate framed by Mt. Fuji. Your guide shares its story.

Free Local landmark

Tea house

### Award-winning tea house

Green tea that has won Japan's Prime Minister's Award, served with seasonal sweets in a hall built from a single 400-year-old tree.

¥1,000 / person Tea & sweets

Local food

### Fujinomiya yakisoba

B-1 Grand Prix soul food with a chewy local noodle, at a family-run spot locals queue for.

¥900 / person Lunch stop

Sweets

### S.gelato

Locally sourced ice cream, with mochi and matcha drinks too — a sweet local stop.

¥500–800 / person Dessert

Brewery

### 190-year-old sake brewery

Sake brewed since the 1830s with pure Mt. Fuji snowmelt, in a working brewery the town grew around. The tasting is the brewery’s courtesy to browsing customers — no obligation to buy.

Free Brewery’s courtesy

Mt. Fuji Exhibits

### Mt. Fuji World Heritage Centre

An inverted Fuji of wood and water; the mountain's whole story told indoors. Our go-to when the weather turns.

¥500 / person Rain-friendly

Shopping

### Traditional clothing shop

Jinbei in classic wave, dragon and floral prints, hung above cases of tenugui hand towels and sashes. A good stop for something you will actually wear at home.

¥1,000+ / item Souvenirs

Shopping

### Hand-made food samples

Japan’s uncanny replica food, made by hand here in Fujinomiya. Sushi, tempura and fruit turned into keychains and magnets — small, light souvenirs that survive the flight home.

¥400–1,000 / item Souvenirs

## Experiences — add any to your booking

### Try Japan's best green tea

Hand-picked, organic, non-fertilised green tea — a Prime Minister's Award winner. Drink it, then season and eat the steeped leaves, with hand-made traditional sweets on the side. Just tea, savoured at the café.

¥1,000 / person 40 min

### Wagashi sweets workshop

Shape seasonal Japanese sweets from white bean paste — nerikiri, a craft born in Edo-period Kyoto two to three centuries ago and refined alongside the tea ceremony.

¥3,000 / person 60 min

### Whisk your own matcha

Learn the traditional preparation under expert guidance, then drink the bowl you made. Tatami or table seating.

¥3,000 / person 60 min

### Tea ceremony with a master

A tea master prepares matcha before you with full explanation — omotenashi in a traditional tea room. Book a month or more ahead.

¥20,000 / group 60 min

### Shinto purification prayer

A traditional oharai ceremony performed by shrine priests inside the main hall — open to everyone.

¥5,000–6,000 / person total 60 min

### Sake brewery tour & tasting

A guided walk inside the working brewery with a tasting of sake made from Mt. Fuji spring water. Offered free as a courtesy — reserve ahead.

Free · tasting incl. 60 min

### Kimono at the shrine

Dress in kimono with professional help and walk the principal Fuji shrine — the scenery does the rest.

¥3,500 / person total 60 min

### Maki Sushi

Roll peach-blossom patterned sushi, an Edo-era festival art — no raw fish. Eat it on-site or take it onto your train.

¥5,500 / person + ¥2,000 / group 60 min

pages.title: About Fuji Soul Tours — Born at the Foot of Mt. Fuji
pages.description: Fuji Soul Tours was founded by Takumu Makino, born and raised at the foot of Mt. Fuji in Fujinomiya. Why we run private, half-day, local-side tours — and who guides them.
pages.text:
About Fuji Soul Tours

# Born at the foot of the mountain

Fuji Soul Tours runs private, half-day cultural tours from Shin-Fuji Station — built by someone who grew up with Mt. Fuji outside the window, for travelers who want the local side of it.

## The founder's story

Takumu (Taku) Makino — founder, born at the mountain's southern foot in Fujinomiya.

I was born and raised at the foot of Mt. Fuji — eighteen years with the mountain as the shape of every morning, not a destination on anyone's itinerary.

Then I left. Four years in Osaka, studying the language and society of Northern Europe; a year interning in Vietnam; six and a half in Tokyo, hosting foreign executives for a multinational company and working alongside colleagues and clients from all over the world. I spent my twenties learning how to make people from somewhere else feel at home in Japan.

What kept catching my eye was how most visitors met Mt. Fuji — herded into 50-seat coaches, photographed at the same three crowded viewpoints, bused back having barely heard a word in their own language. For the people who grew up here, the mountain isn't a backdrop. It's a presence, a weather system, a deity in some senses, a story your grandmother told you.

"I want guests to leave knowing why this mountain matters here — not just that it's tall."

The shape of every morning — dawn over the rooftops of the southern foot.

So I came home, and started curating the parts and pieces of this place I love most into a four-hour day . Private. Slow. Local-side. Bilingual. Built around your schedule, not ours. Maximum five guests, because past that you stop being on a trip and start being on a tour.

These days I'm less often the one guiding — that's deliberate. The tours run with two bilingual guides I work with: same routes, same instincts, same stories to tell. The standard is the one I'd want if I were the guest.

Founder Takumu (Taku) Makino

Born At the foot of Mt. Fuji's southern face — Fujinomiya

Languages English · Japanese (native bilingual)

Before this Osaka · Vietnam · Tokyo — hosting foreign executives for a multinational company

## Who guides your day

Every tour is led by one of two bilingual guides Takumu works with — a consistent pair, not a freelance pool. Same hidden viewpoints, same family-run lunch spots, same instinct for reading the weather and rerouting by the hour. You'll be told who your guide is before the tour.

## What we mean by "Soul"

It's the word in our name, and it's a promise about how we guide: every stop comes with its why . Why most Japanese visit shrines without being religious, why the streets stay spotless with no trash cans, why everything at the mountain's foot tastes of its water — we wrote the whole philosophy down here .

pages.title: Mt. Fuji Stopover Between Tokyo & Kyoto: The Shin-Fuji Guide
pages.description: How to see Mt. Fuji in half a day when moving between Tokyo and Kyoto: hop off the Shinkansen at Shin-Fuji Station. Trains, luggage, sample timetables and what to do.
pages.text:
Travel guide

# Mt. Fuji between Tokyo and Kyoto: the stopover guide

You're taking the Shinkansen — the bullet train — from Tokyo to Kyoto (or back) and wondering if you can fit Mt. Fuji in without losing a day. You can — in half a day, with your luggage. Here's exactly how the Shin-Fuji stopover works.

## Why a stopover beats a day trip

Most travelers see Mt. Fuji on a full-day bus tour from Tokyo : two to three hours out, the same back, and a whole day of your itinerary gone. But the Tokaido Shinkansen — the bullet train you're already taking between Tokyo and Kyoto — passes right by the mountain's southern foot.

Shin-Fuji Station sits about an hour from Tokyo and roughly two hours from Kyoto. Step off mid-journey, spend four hours at the mountain, and board a later train onward. You arrive in Kyoto (or Tokyo) the same evening, having traded a travel day for a Mt. Fuji day. That's the entire trick.

The southern side of Mt. Fuji — all of this sits within reach of Shin-Fuji Station.

## The trains: what to know before you book

- Only the Kodama (こだま) stops at Shin-Fuji — not the Nozomi or Hikari. The Kodama is the all-stations service: slower overall, usually less crowded, and covered by the JR Pass.
- Book through SmartEX (smart-ex.jp), JR's official Shinkansen booking site — it lists all stations including Shin-Fuji and has the best change and cancellation terms. Many third-party apps simply don't show Shin-Fuji because the Nozomi skips it.
- Window seats for Fuji views from the train: seat E heading from Tokyo, seat A heading from Kyoto or Osaka.
- If you're on a Nozomi, you can transfer to a Kodama at Shizuoka or Mishima — your guide can help you plan connections after booking.

## What about luggage?

This is the question everyone asks, and it's the easiest one. On a private tour , the van stores large cases for up to three guests — your bags ride with you. Bigger groups use the coin lockers at Shin-Fuji Station (¥300–800, cash). Either way, you walk back onto your train with everything you arrived with.

The private van's cargo space — room for your cases while you tour.

## Sample stopover timetables

These are example timings — after booking, you send us your train times and the day is planned around them. We ask for a 30-minute buffer between tour end and your train's departure; since Kodama trains run only about twice an hour, a station wait of up to an hour is normal (or extend the tour instead — see the FAQ ).

Route | Step off | Tour | Back on board | Arrive

Tokyo → Kyoto | Depart Tokyo 6:57, arrive Shin-Fuji 8:03 | 8:10–12:10 | 13:08 | Kyoto 15:15 — full evening ahead
Kyoto → Tokyo | Depart Kyoto 8:30, arrive Shin-Fuji 10:36 | 10:45–14:45 | 15:38 | Tokyo 16:46 — in time for dinner
Tokyo round trip | Depart Tokyo 6:57, arrive Shin-Fuji 8:03 | 8:10–12:10 | 13:10 | Tokyo 14:18 — afternoon free

## What can you actually do in four hours?

Guests at a park viewpoint mid-tour — four hours is more than it sounds.

More than you'd think, because everything sits close to the station on the quiet southern side of the mountain:

- Hidden viewpoints — chosen the morning of your visit for the clearest angle on the mountain ( here's how locals avoid the crowds )
- Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha — the principal shrine of Mt. Fuji worship, where climbs traditionally began
- Fujinomiya yakisoba — the region's B-1 Grand Prix–winning soul food, at a family-run shop ( full story here )
- Green tea or matcha at an award-winning tea house built from a single 400-year-old tree

You can do this independently with taxis and patience — or as a private half-day tour where a local-born bilingual guide meets you at the ticket gate, drives the day, and has you back on the platform with buffer to spare. Either way, the stopover is worth it.

## Mt. Fuji stopover FAQ

faq.q: Can you stop at Mt. Fuji on the bullet train between Tokyo and Kyoto?
faq.a: Yes. The Tokaido Shinkansen — the bullet train between Tokyo and Kyoto — passes the southern foot of Mt. Fuji, and the all-stations Kodama service stops at Shin-Fuji Station, about an hour from Tokyo and roughly two from Kyoto. Step off mid-journey, spend about four hours at the mountain, and board a later train onward the same day.

faq.q: Which bullet train stops near Mt. Fuji?
faq.a: Only the Kodama (こだま) stops at Shin-Fuji Station — not the Nozomi or Hikari. It is covered by the JR Pass and is usually less crowded. Book through SmartEX, JR's official site, which lists Shin-Fuji; many third-party apps hide the stop because the Nozomi skips it.

faq.q: How long do you need for a Mt. Fuji stopover?
faq.a: About four hours on the ground is enough, because everything sits close to Shin-Fuji Station on the quiet southern side — a viewpoint, the Fujisan Hongu Sengen shrine, Fujinomiya yakisoba and a teahouse all fit comfortably before your onward train.

faq.q: Can I do the Mt. Fuji stopover with my luggage?
faq.a: Yes. On a private tour the van carries large cases for up to three guests, so your bags ride with you. Bigger groups use the coin lockers at Shin-Fuji Station (¥300–800, cash). Either way you board your next train with everything you arrived with.

faq.q: Do I need a tour, or can I do the Shin-Fuji stopover on my own?
faq.a: You can do it independently with taxis and some planning. A private half-day tour removes the friction — a local-born bilingual guide meets you at the ticket gate, drives the day, stores your luggage, and has you back on the platform with time to spare.

pages.title: How to See Mt. Fuji Without the Crowds — a Local's Guide
pages.description: Skip the tour-bus viewpoints. A local's guide to seeing Mt. Fuji without the crowds: the quiet southern side, when visibility is best, and what to do if the mountain hides.
pages.text:
Local's guide

# How to see Mt. Fuji without the crowds

The famous viewpoints come with tour buses, tripod queues and convenience-store barricades. Locals see the same mountain in peace — by standing on the other side of it. Here's how.

## The trick: switch sides

Nearly all international tourism concentrates on Mt. Fuji's northern side — the Kawaguchiko lakes and the famous pagoda shot. The photos are real, and so are the crowds that come with every tour bus from Tokyo.

The southern side — Fujinomiya, at the mountain's foot — is where Fuji worship historically began and where locals actually live with the mountain. It has its own lakes-and-plateau viewpoints, the principal shrine of Fuji worship, and a fraction of the visitors, because the big buses don't come here. It's also the easy side to reach if you're already on the Tokyo–Kyoto Shinkansen: Shin-Fuji Station is right there .

A park viewpoint on the southern side — a bench, the mountain, and nobody fighting for the shot.

## Go where the locals point you

On the southern side the best angle changes with the day — cloud cover, season, snowline. Locals keep a mental list of spots and pick on the morning itself. Ours runs to seven local viewpoints : a bridge that frames the peak, a highland plateau with grazing cows, a lakeside "double Fuji" mirror reflection, a quiet park bench above the city, and yes — a convenience-store shot without the barricades and crowds of the famous one.

That morning-of flexibility is the real luxury. A fixed itinerary drives to a viewpoint and hopes; a local picks the viewpoint that's working today .

The lakeside "double Fuji" — and an empty deck to see it from.

The highland plateau — cows, grass, and the mountain to yourself.

## When can you actually see Mt. Fuji?

Honest numbers, because the mountain hides more often than brochures admit:

Season | Chance of seeing Mt. Fuji

November – February | Best — roughly 60–73% of days
Spring & Fall | Roughly 27–47% of days
Summer | Shyest — roughly 13–17% of days

Two rules of thumb apply year-round: mornings beat afternoons (clouds build over the day), and a clear winter morning is about as close to a guarantee as Fuji ever gives.

Spring, just after sunrise — first light on the snowcap, cherry blossoms below.

## And if the mountain hides?

Plan for it rather than gamble. The southern side is dense with indoor and cultural experiences that don't depend on visibility: a special prayer inside Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha , the UNESCO World Heritage Center that tells the mountain's story indoors, sake tasting at a 190-year-old brewery , and an award-winning tea house . On our tours this isn't a consolation prize — rainy-day guests regularly leave five-star reviews. The cloudy-day plan is laid out on the tour page .

pages.title: Fujinomiya Yakisoba: Mt. Fuji's B-1 Grand Prix Soul Food
pages.description: Fujinomiya yakisoba won Japan's first national B-1 Grand Prix — and you can only get the real thing at the foot of Mt. Fuji. What makes it different and where locals eat it.
pages.text:
Local food

# Fujinomiya yakisoba: the champion soul food of Mt. Fuji's foot

Japan ranks its regional comfort foods in a national competition — and the noodles from this small city at the foot of Mt. Fuji took the very first crown. Here's what makes them different, and where locals actually eat them.

## What is Fujinomiya yakisoba?

Yakisoba — stir-fried noodles with vegetables, meat and a savory sauce — exists all over Japan. But Fujinomiya yakisoba is its own protected style, born in this one city and famously hard to replicate elsewhere.

What sets it apart: noticeably firm, chewy noodles made by local makers using the area's cold Mt. Fuji spring water; niku-kasu (savory pork cracklings) fried into the mix instead of plain oil; and a finishing dusting of dried sardine-and-mackerel powder instead of the usual seaweed flakes. The result is chewier, smokier and more savory than yakisoba anywhere else in Japan.

Griddled to order — firm noodles, pork cracklings, fish powder. ~¥900 at a family-run shop.

## The B-1 Grand Prix story

The B-1 Grand Prix is Japan's national championship of B-kyu gurume — "B-class gourmet," the cheap, beloved everyday dishes that locals are proudest of. When the first nationwide competition was held in 2006, Fujinomiya yakisoba won it. Then it won again in 2007. Two consecutive national titles put this small city on Japan's food map for good, and the dish remains the benchmark every other B-1 contender is measured against.

For Fujinomiya, it was never a gimmick: the noodles have been griddled at family-run shops and shotengai stalls here since the post-war years. The competition just told the rest of Japan what locals already knew.

## Where to eat it like a local

Follow the orange banners — yakisoba shops cluster around Fujinomiya's old center.

You'll find Fujinomiya yakisoba around the city's old center near Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha , the principal shrine of Mt. Fuji worship — many shops griddle it to order on a flat teppan in front of you, and a generous plate runs about ¥900 .

On our private half-day tour , lunch is at a family-run spot that locals queue for — the kind of place with a handful of seats and a teppan that's been seasoned by decades of service. Your guide orders, explains what you're eating and why it matters here, and handles the Japanese. It's consistently one of the most-mentioned moments in our guest reviews .

## Fitting it into your trip

Fujinomiya — the mountain is part of the streetscape here.

Fujinomiya sits at Mt. Fuji's southern foot, about 30 minutes from Shin-Fuji Station on the Tokyo–Kyoto Shinkansen line. If you're traveling between the two cities, you can step off, spend half a day at the mountain — viewpoints, the shrine, yakisoba lunch, a 400-year-old tea house — and continue the same day. Our stopover guide covers the trains, luggage and timings.

pages.title: Mt. Fuji Green Tea: Shizuoka's Quiet Tea Culture at the Mountain's Foot
pages.description: At the foot of Mt. Fuji lies Shizuoka, Japan's tea country. Taste award-winning sencha the slow way — one cup, low and unhurried, with a seasonal sweet, in a 400-year-old wooden hall.
pages.text:
Local culture

# Green tea at the foot of Mt. Fuji

Most visitors come to Mt. Fuji for the mountain. Its southern foot hides a quieter pleasure: sencha — Japan's everyday green tea, grown in the country's most famous tea region and best tasted slowly, far from the crowds.

## Shizuoka — Japan's tea country

Shizuoka isn't as famous abroad as Tokyo or Kyoto, but to Japan it's tea country. The prefecture grows roughly one-third to 40% of the nation's green tea , depending on how you measure it — about 36% of all crude tea and 41% of sencha in recent figures. The city at Mt. Fuji's southern foot is a tea town in its own right, where tea is the top crop by planted area and many growers still do everything themselves — growing, processing and selling their own leaf. It's raised on the clean water and air of the mountain; in places the tea fields and Fuji sit in a single view.

## A tea garden that values care over scale

The garden we visit isn't a big commercial operation. It's a family-run tea garden, around sixty years old, that grows, processes and sells its own tea by hand — less factory, more small estate, closer to the way a small winery makes its wine. The leaf is hand-picked, grown without chemical fertilizer, and taken from the first soft sprouts of the season , the tenderest and most fragrant part of the plant. None of it is showy — and yet the garden's tea has won Japan's Prime Minister's Award, among other national honors. Premium, but not flashy: exactly the kind of local, uncrowded place that's hard to find on your own.

## One cup, served slow and low

This isn't a quick cup from a vending machine, and it isn't bitter the way many visitors expect — made from hand-picked young leaves, it's soft, deeply fragrant and rich in umami . You're served a single, carefully prepared tea — one type, one cup — and shown how to draw the best from it. A small lidded cup holds about four grams of leaf. The first pour is deliberately cool, around 40°C, coaxing out sweetness and aroma rather than bitterness; you sip it through a narrow gap between the lid and the cup. Then a little hotter water for a second steeping, hotter again for a third, so the same leaf shows a different face each time — a slow, attentive way to taste how one tea changes.

## A seasonal sweet, made by hand

The tea doesn't come alone. With it comes a hand-made Japanese sweet — usually nerikiri , sweet white-bean paste shaped into the flowers of the moment: hydrangea in the rainy season, cherry blossom in spring. It isn't just something sweet; it's a small, edible expression of the season. Tasting the umami of the tea against its gentle sweetness carries one of the quiet ideas at the heart of Japanese culture — that you eat and drink the season, not just the food.

## Then you eat the leaves

Here's the part that surprises even Japanese guests: you eat the tea leaves. Most green tea leaves are made only for steeping, never for eating. But when the leaf is this tender — young, hand-picked, top grade — the steeped leaves become a small dish of their own. After the final infusion they're lifted into a bowl and seasoned with soy sauce, a little bonito, sometimes a touch of yuzu. Green tea you don't just drink, but eat.

## A room built from a single 400-year-old tree

The setting is part of it. The café sits in a traditional wooden hall built — remarkably — from a single 400-year-old Japanese cedar , a trunk so vast it would take five adults with arms outstretched to circle it. Like Japan's old shrines and temples, it's joined with interlocking woodwork and almost no nails or metal. Nothing here is grand or decorative; it's minimal, calm and full of empty space — which suits a tea that's about subtlety, not spectacle: fine aroma, umami, the shift of temperature, the feel of the season.

Coming all this way for Mt. Fuji and only looking at the mountain would be a shame. At its foot is a green-tea culture shaped by the same water, air and climate — the local, unhurried side of Fuji that most visitors never reach.

pages.title: The Soul of Things: Why Japan Is the Way It Is | Fuji Soul Tours
pages.description: Why do Japanese visit shrines without being religious? Why are the streets spotless with no trash cans? We try to tell the soul of things — the invisible forces behind what you'll see in Japan.
pages.text:
Our philosophy

# We try to tell the soul of things

It's the word in our name. Most tours show you what Japan looks like; we'd rather you leave knowing why it is the way it is — the invisible forces behind the shrine, the spotless street, the mountain itself.

## What "soul" means here

The mountain over a temple gate on the quiet southern side — presence, not backdrop.

For the people who grew up at its foot, Mt. Fuji isn't a backdrop. It's a presence, a weather system, a deity in some senses, a story your grandmother told you. That gap — between the mountain on a postcard and the mountain as it's actually lived with — is what Fuji Soul Tours was built to close .

So on tour, every stop comes with its why . Why this shrine is where Fuji worship began. Why the tea house has stood for centuries. Why locals queue at a particular yakisoba griddle. You can photograph Japan in a day; understanding even a small piece of it is what you'll still be talking about years later.

## Why do most Japanese visit shrines — without considering themselves religious?

Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha — the principal shrine of Mt. Fuji worship.

Many Japanese people don't identify as religious in a Western sense — yet nearly everyone visits shrines on New Year's, attends Buddhist funerals, and prays at temples for good luck. How?

Shinto and Buddhism in Japan are not competing belief systems — they've coexisted and blended for over 1,400 years. Shinto, rooted in the idea that gods (kami) dwell in nature — mountains, rivers, trees — is less a set of doctrines than a way of relating to the world. Buddhism, which arrived from China in the 6th century, added a framework for life's rituals: birth, death, the afterlife.

The result is a culture where spiritual practice is habitual and communal, not confessional. You don't need to "believe" to participate — just as people around the world celebrate Christmas without being devout. For most Japanese, visiting Mt. Fuji's shrine isn't an act of faith; it's an act of being Japanese.

On tour, your guide shows the small courtesies — how to bow, purify your hands, and pay respects.

## Why are Japan's streets so clean — with almost no public trash cans?

Japan removed most public trash cans in the 1990s following security concerns — yet streets stayed immaculate. Visitors are often baffled. The answer isn't enforcement. It's three overlapping worldviews that have shaped behavior for centuries:

- Shinto: 清浄 (purity) — spaces, especially sacred ones, must be kept clean and pure. A cluttered, dirty space is one where kami cannot dwell. The habit extends from the shrine to the street.
- Zen Buddhism: cleaning as practice (修行) — in Zen temples, sweeping and scrubbing are not chores but meditation. Japanese schools still begin the day with students cleaning their own classrooms.
- Confucian 和 (harmony) — one should not impose burden on others. Leaving litter isn't just untidy; it's a disruption of collective harmony. So people carry their trash home.

No single force explains it. It's the intersection of all three — and once you see it, you see it everywhere in Japan.

## Why everything here tastes of the mountain

Spring water from the mountain feeds the gardens, breweries and tea fields below it.

One more thread ties the whole region together: water. Snow that falls on Mt. Fuji filters down through volcanic rock and emerges at its southern foot as some of Japan's purest spring water. It's why a 190-year-old brewery makes sake here, why the local tea is good enough to win national awards, and why Fujinomiya's noodle makers credit the water for their yakisoba. Drink anything on the southern side and, in a real sense, you're tasting the mountain.
